slides.title: Why Coding?
slides.say: Welcome everyone and thank them for coming. Introduce yourself and your role in running the course. Set expectations: about 25 minutes of talk, then questions. Say up front that you will be honest about what research does and does not show: this is not a sales pitch, and nothing tonight promises jobs, grades or college places.
slides.plain: The illustration is original: colored blocks (like Scratch) on the left turn into lines of typed code on the right. That is the journey the children take in this course.

qa.q: Do I need to know anything about computers to follow tonight?
qa.a: No. Every technical word is explained, and you never need to code to help your child.

slides.title: Computing is changing the skills our kids need
slides.source: World Economic Forum (2025), a survey of over 1,000 employers.
slides.say: The World Economic Forum surveys large employers worldwide every two years. In the January 2025 report, the three skills expected to grow fastest by 2030 are AI and big data; networks and cybersecurity; and technological literacy. Analytical thinking remains the skill employers most often call essential (seven in ten). Stress the take-away: we are not trying to turn ten-year-olds into software engineers. We want them to understand, question and shape the technology they will grow up with.
slides.plain: This is a survey of what employers expect, not a measurement of the future. Forecasts like this are useful for direction, not for precise predictions.

qa.q: Will coding guarantee my child a good job?
qa.a: No, and nobody can promise that. What we can say is that understanding how computers and AI work is becoming a basic literacy, like understanding money or science.

slides.title: Schools are still catching up
slides.source: Code.org et al. (2025); national data, 2024–25 school year.
slides.say: These are the latest national figures from the annual State of Computer Science Education report (Code.org with the Computer Science Teachers Association and the ECEP Alliance), published December 2025. About 60 percent of public high schools offered a foundational computer science course, and about 6 percent of high school students were enrolled in one. The share of schools offering it has flattened compared with earlier years. The point is not that schools are failing; it is that most children will meet very little computer science in school, so a gentle start at home can help.
slides.plain: These numbers describe US public high schools. Elementary schools are measured differently, so we do not quote a figure for them. Local schools may be better or worse than the national picture.

qa.q: Does our local school teach coding?
qa.a: It varies a lot by school. It is worth asking; our course works alongside school, not instead of it.

slides.title: With AI, understanding code matters more
slides.say: Many parents ask: if AI can write code, why learn? Two pieces of evidence. First, a controlled study at the University of Toronto with 69 learners aged 10 to 17: half had an AI code generator while learning Python. Those with AI completed more tasks and scored higher while learning, and they did not get worse at editing code by hand. A week later, on tests without AI, the difference was small and not statistically significant. Second, the OECD’s 2026 Digital Education Outlook warns that general-purpose chatbots can raise performance on tasks without producing lasting learning, while tools designed for learning (giving hints, asking questions) do better. Our course uses no online AI tools; in Level 3 the children build tiny AI models by hand so they understand how AI learns and where it fails.
slides.plain: “Not statistically significant” means the difference was small enough that it could be down to chance. One study of 69 children cannot settle the question.

qa.q: Should my child use ChatGPT for homework?
qa.a: Not for this course. The homework is about thinking through the problem; we teach how AI works in Level 3 instead.

slides.title: What coding builds, and how sure we are
slides.source: Scherer et al. (2019); Scherer et al. (2020); Montuori et al. (2024); Wing (2006).
slides.say: This slide is the honest summary of the whole evidence section. Read the rows from top to bottom: we are most confident about what is closest to coding itself. Children reliably learn to program and to think in steps. There is good evidence for gains in problem solving and planning, especially on tasks that resemble coding. Effects on math, creativity and reasoning are positive on average but shrink in the most careful studies, so we call them mixed. Reading and school grades benefit least. Whether coding builds general persistence or teamwork is an open question: few studies measure it well.
slides.plain: Each badge uses a color, an icon and a word, so it reads the same in black and white. “Strong” means several careful studies and reviews agree. “Mixed” means results vary or shrink with stronger study designs. “Open” means we simply do not know yet.

qa.q: So will it help with math?
qa.a: Possibly a little, and especially with problem solving, but we do not promise better math grades. Think of it as its own valuable subject.

slides.title: The biggest review: 105 studies
slides.source: Scherer et al. (2019) (105 studies, 539 effects); Scherer et al. (2020).
slides.say: This is the largest review of whether learning to program helps other kinds of thinking. Scherer, Siddiq and Sánchez Viveros combined 105 studies with 539 results. Skills closest to programming improved most. Gains also appeared for creative thinking, math and metacognition (thinking about your own thinking), and to a lesser degree spatial skills and reasoning. Reading and school achievement benefited least. Importantly, studies that compared coders with children who did nothing at all found bigger effects than studies with an active comparison group, and published studies showed bigger effects than unpublished ones. That is a reason to be modest. A companion review by the same team (2020, 139 interventions) found a large effect of teaching on programming skill itself.
slides.plain: A meta-analysis pools many studies to find the overall pattern. When effects get smaller in better-designed studies, part of the “benefit” in weaker studies may come from simply doing something new and fun, not from coding itself.

qa.q: What is “thinking about thinking”?
qa.a: Metacognition: noticing how you are solving a problem and changing strategy when it isn’t working. Debugging practices exactly this.

slides.alt: Slide 7: WHAT THE RESEARCH SHOWS The biggest review: 105 studies Children reliably learn to program when taught. Some gains spread: creative thinking, math, thinking about thinking. Smaller gains for spatial skills and reasoning. Least benefit: reading and school grades. Stronger study designs found smaller effects. Lightbulb Take-away Expect better coders and problem solvers, not…

slides.title: Where coding seems to help most
slides.source: Montuori et al. (2024); pooled (fixed-effect) estimates from 11 studies.
slides.say: This 2024 review looked only at experiments with children: 19 studies with 1,523 participants, of which 11 could be combined. The pooled effects were large for problem solving (0.89), smaller for planning (0.36), and small for working memory (0.20) and inhibition, the ability to stop an automatic response (0.17). The dashed lines show common rules of thumb: 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.
slides.plain: An effect size compares the average improvement of the coding group with the comparison group, in units of how spread out children’s scores are. 0.89 means a big difference; 0.17 a small one. Because the review pooled only 11 studies, we label it mixed rather than strong.

qa.q: Is 0.89 a lot?
qa.a: Yes, it is large by usual standards, but it comes from a small number of studies, so treat it as promising rather than proven.

slides.title: A closer look: one fair test
slides.source: Arfé et al. (2020), a cluster-randomized controlled trial.
slides.say: This is one of the cleanest studies in the field. Researchers in Italy randomly assigned ten first-grade classes either to eight hours of coding over four weeks (using Code.org puzzles) or to their usual STEM lessons. Before and after, children did planning puzzles such as the Tower of London and tests of inhibition, the ability to stop an automatic response. The coding group improved more, especially in planning; the effect on inhibition was smaller.
slides.plain: Random assignment is the gold standard: because chance decides who codes, differences at the end are much more likely to be caused by the coding itself. Still, it is one short study of six-year-olds, so we should not assume the same size of effect for our ten-year-olds.

qa.q: Why show a study of six-year-olds?
qa.a: Because it is one of the few truly randomized trials. Studies of older children mostly point the same way but with weaker designs.

slides.title: Early experiences shape interest
slides.source: Master et al. (2017); Tai et al. (2006); Google & Gallup (2016).
slides.say: Three findings about interest. First, in a University of Washington experiment, first graders who programmed a small robot showed no gender gap in technology interest and confidence afterwards, while in the comparison groups boys reported more of both. The short activity did not change children’s stereotypes, though. Second, a large US study followed students from eighth grade (1988) into college: those who expected a science-related career at age 13 to 14 were roughly two to three times as likely to graduate with a science degree. This is a correlation (an association), not proof that early interest causes the degree. Third, a 2016 Google–Gallup survey found girls are less likely than boys to be told by parents and teachers that they would be good at computer science.
slides.plain: Correlation versus causation: children who already love science might both expect a science career and later study it. The early expectation might not cause the degree; it might just be an early sign of it. The 2006 study is also old (data from 1988 to 2000).

qa.q: My daughter says coding is for boys. What can I do?
qa.a: Encourage her as much as you would a son, and point out the variety of people who code. Our course never assigns roles by gender.

slides.title: What we don't know (yet)
slides.source: Pea & Kurland (1984) (an early critique); Sala & Gobet (2017); Scherer et al. (2019).
slides.say: This is the most important slide for trust. Researchers have argued about this since the 1980s: Pea and Kurland at Bank Street College questioned the hope that programming automatically improves general thinking, and early studies with the Logo language were disappointing when there was no deliberate teaching. (That critique is old, which we flag, but its lesson still holds.) A 2017 review of chess, music and memory training found the same general pattern: skills rarely carry over to unrelated areas, and apparent effects shrink in better-designed studies. So our promise is modest: children will become capable, confident beginner programmers and practice problem solving. Anything beyond that is a bonus.
slides.plain: “Transfer” means using a skill learned in one area somewhere else. Near transfer (to similar problems) is common; far transfer (to unrelated subjects) is rare for any activity.

qa.q: Then why bother?
qa.a: Because coding is worth learning for its own sake, like music or a language, and because the way we teach it (projects, teamwork, debugging) builds good learning habits.

slides.title: Six principles the evidence supports
slides.say: Research is clearer about how to teach coding than about its spill-over benefits. These six principles come up again and again. The next three slides give the evidence for each, and then we show where each one appears in our course. The small label in the corner of each card names the key source.

qa.q: Is there one best way to teach coding?
qa.a: No single method wins everywhere, but these ingredients are consistently linked to better learning and motivation.

slides.title: Create, don't just consume
slides.source: Papert (1980); Resnick et al. (2009); Lee et al. (2011).
slides.say: Seymour Papert at MIT argued in 1980 that children learn best by building things that matter to them. The Scratch team (Resnick and colleagues, 2009) turned this into three design goals: a low floor (easy to start), a high ceiling (room for complex projects) and wide walls (many kinds of project, so every child finds an interest). Lee and colleagues (2011) describe a progression called Use–Modify–Create: first play with a working program, then change it, then design your own. Our lessons follow exactly that pattern.
slides.plain: These are design principles from experienced researchers rather than results of one experiment. They are widely used in computing education because they keep children engaged.

qa.q: My child only wants to make games. Is that OK?
qa.a: Yes. Games are a great vehicle: they need loops, conditions, variables and debugging. Art and data projects are there for others.

slides.title: Learn together, fix bugs on purpose
slides.source: Umapathy & Ritzhaupt (2017); Denner et al. (2014); Michaeli & Romeike (2019); Wisniewski et al. (2020).
slides.say: Pair programming means two children share one computer: the driver types, the navigator reads, plans and spots mistakes, and they swap regularly. A 2017 review of 18 studies (mostly university courses) found better results for pairs on assignments, exams and staying in the course, though not on attitudes. A study of 320 middle-school students (Denner and colleagues, 2014) found pairs gained more programming knowledge, especially children with less experience. Debugging: a German classroom study found that explicitly teaching a systematic process for finding bugs improved both debugging performance and students’ confidence compared with practice alone. Feedback: a 2020 review of 435 studies found a solid medium-sized effect on learning, largest when feedback gives information about the task and how to improve, and smaller for praise alone.
slides.plain: You may hear a famous figure of 0.79 for feedback (Hattie and Timperley, 2007). A later, larger re-analysis by the same research group found about 0.48, which is still a solid effect. We quote the more careful estimate qualitatively.

qa.q: What if my child does not get along with their partner?
qa.a: We rotate pairs, set clear roles and swap every few minutes. With an odd number, a trio uses driver, navigator and tester.

slides.title: Off-screen first, read before writing, return often
slides.source: Olmo-Muñoz et al. (2020); Sentance et al. (2019); Bruner (1960).
slides.say: Unplugged activities teach computing ideas without a computer: acting out a loop as a dance, sorting cards, giving a parent-robot exact instructions. A Spanish study with early primary pupils found that starting with unplugged activities before moving to the computer helped computational thinking and motivation. PRIMM (Predict, Run, Investigate, Modify, Make) asks students to read and predict what code does before writing their own; an evaluation in 13 UK schools with 493 students aged 11 to 14 found better post-test results than a comparison group. The spiral curriculum idea comes from psychologist Jerome Bruner (1960): return to big ideas repeatedly, at greater depth each time.
slides.plain: Reading code before writing it is like reading books before writing stories: it builds a picture of how programs work, so writing becomes less frustrating.

qa.q: Isn’t time away from the computer wasted?
qa.a: No. Off-screen activities make the ideas concrete and give eyes a break; they are short and always lead into building.

slides.title: How our course puts this into practice
slides.source: Course design (docs/DESIGN.md, docs/SYLLABUS.md); per-level minimums are checked automatically.
slides.say: This slide links research to practice. Every one of the 42 sessions follows the same five-part shape. The minimums in this table (per level: at least six unplugged activities, ten bug hunts, ten pair-programming activities and ten free-build times) are checked automatically by the course’s quality tests, so they cannot quietly disappear when material is edited. Each lesson includes a support path for children who need more time and an extension path for those who finish early. Many lessons ask children to predict what code will do before running it.
slides.plain: An “exit check” is a quick question at the end of a session that shows whether the idea landed, so the next session can adjust.

qa.q: What if my child is ahead or behind the others?
qa.a: Every lesson has an easier route and a stretch challenge, and two optional spare sessions per level give time to catch up within the 12 weeks.

slides.title: Why blocks first, then Python
slides.source: Weintrop & Wilensky (2017); Weintrop & Wilensky (2019); Xu et al. (2019).
slides.say: Scratch, created at MIT, uses snap-together blocks, so children cannot make spelling or bracket mistakes. In a high school study by Weintrop and Wilensky, students using a block-based tool scored higher on concept tests after the first five weeks than students using an equivalent text tool. When both groups then moved to a professional text language (Java), the difference disappeared: blocks gave no harm and no lasting advantage. A 2019 review of 13 studies found a small advantage for blocks that was not statistically significant. Our choice: blocks for the first six weeks while ideas like loops and events are new, then Python, a real language used by professionals, with every Scratch idea re-taught in text.
slides.plain: The chart shows one estimate (the dot) and its range of plausible values (the line). Because the line crosses zero, the true effect could be zero. That is why we call it mixed, and why we switch to text quickly instead of staying with blocks for a long time.

qa.q: Isn’t Scratch just a toy?
qa.a: It is a real programming language with the same core ideas; we use it as a ramp, and move to Python after six weeks.

slides.title: The roadmap: three levels of 10--12 weeks
slides.say: Walk along the timeline. Each level runs 10 to 12 weeks, one session a week, so all three levels take 30 to 36 weeks of sessions; weeks we skip for holidays do not count. The standard plan is 12 sessions; in the 10-week plan two pairs of weeks are combined into single sessions, with the rest of that work done as homework. Two ready-made spare sessions are optional and only used if there is room inside the 12 weeks. Inside every level the rhythm is the same: new ideas in weeks 1 to 5, a review and friendly checkpoint in week 6, more new ideas in weeks 7 to 9, a final project in weeks 10 and 11, and a showcase in week 12. Families can decide level by level whether to continue.

qa.q: Do we have to commit to all three levels?
qa.a: No. Each level ends with a complete project and a certificate; you decide about the next level then.

slides.title: Level 1: Introduction
slides.source: Level 1 syllabus; aligned with CSTA standards for grades 3–5 (Computer Science Teachers Association, 2017).
slides.say: Level 1 starts from zero. Weeks 1 to 6 use Scratch blocks: making sprites move, draw patterns, react to keys, and keep score in simple games. Week 6 is review and a friendly checkpoint. Weeks 7 to 12 move to Python, using the turtle, which draws on screen: the same ideas, now typed. The final project, My Interactive Art Show, must use a question, a variable, an if, a loop, something random and a function the child wrote. Children who need more time can build it in Scratch with the same rubric.
slides.plain: A “variable” is a labeled box that remembers something, like a score. A “function” is a named mini-program you can reuse, like a recipe card.

qa.q: Is typing a problem for a ten-year-old?
qa.a: Programs at this level are short; we start very small, and typing improves quickly.

slides.title: Level 2: Intermediate
slides.source: Level 2 syllabus; aligned with CSTA standards for grades 6–8 (Computer Science Teachers Association, 2017).
slides.say: Level 2 is all Python. Children learn to organize code into functions that return answers, store many values in lists and dictionaries, save data to files, and, a highlight, write automatic tests that prove their code works. They build keyboard-driven games and generative art. A short placement quiz in week 1 helps tailor support; it is never a pass or fail. The final project is a choice between an arcade game and an art studio, with at least three tests the child writes.
slides.plain: A “test” is a tiny program that checks another program gives the right answer, like a spell-checker for logic. Professionals use them every day.

qa.q: What if my child struggled with Level 1?
qa.a: The placement quiz and Level 1 review show where to start; repeating parts of Level 1 is completely fine.

slides.title: Level 3: Advanced
slides.source: Level 3 syllabus; AI topics follow the AI4K12 Five Big Ideas (Touretzky et al., 2019).
slides.say: Level 3 introduces the ideas behind larger programs: classes and objects (blueprints and things built from them), searching and sorting, recursion for fractal art, analyzing a small made-up data set, and how simple AI learns from examples, and copies their mistakes. The children build a tiny AI (a nearest-neighbor classifier) by hand rather than using online AI services, so no data leaves the computer. They also use git, the tool professionals use to save versions of their code; the final project needs at least five tests and eight meaningful git commits. The AI topics follow the AI4K12 framework from AAAI and CSTA; some Level 3 goals borrow from the grades 9–10 standards on purpose.
slides.plain: A “nearest-neighbor classifier” guesses what something is by finding the most similar example it has seen, which shows children exactly why biased examples give biased answers.

qa.q: Isn’t this too advanced for 11-year-olds?
qa.a: It is challenging by design, with step-by-step support. By Level 3 the children have 20 to 24 weeks of practice behind them.

slides.title: What a 60-minute session looks like
slides.say: Every session has the same five parts, so children always know what is coming: a warm-up game (often unplugged), one new idea with a kid-friendly analogy, a short live demo, about 24 minutes building in pairs with a few minutes of free building, and a wrap-up where children show their work and answer a quick exit question. Homework takes 15 to 20 minutes a week, with a core task for everyone and optional challenge and creative extras; none needs the internet. Equipment: a Mac with the free Scratch app and Thonny. In Level 2 a testing tool called pytest is installed once (internet needed once, no account), and Level 3 uses Apple’s free command-line tools for git.

qa.q: We don’t have a Mac at home. Is that a problem?
qa.a: No. Paper parts of the homework work at the kitchen table, and computer tasks can be finished at the next session.

slides.title: What success looks like
slides.say: These are realistic outcomes, not guarantees: children progress at different rates. Each level has a short, friendly checkpoint in week 6 and an exit check in week 12, plus a project rubric with four levels. The rubric values three things equally: making the project their own, making it work, and being able to explain it. Scores are used to decide what support to offer next, never as grades.
slides.plain: A “rubric” is a simple chart that describes what each level of work looks like, so children can see what “better” means and assess themselves.

qa.q: Will I get a report?
qa.a: You will see the project at each showcase and can ask for the checkpoint and rubric results; there is also a progress tracker children fill in.

slides.title: How you can help, no coding needed
slides.source: Google & Gallup (2016); Master et al. (2017); Wisniewski et al. (2020).
slides.say: None of this needs any coding knowledge. Asking for a demo makes your child the expert, which builds confidence. Asking about bugs signals that mistakes are normal and interesting. Praising strategies (“you tried three ways to fix that”) gives more useful feedback than labels like “you’re a natural”. A regular 15-minute slot is easier than a long weekend session. Encouraging daughters and sons equally matters because surveys show girls hear less encouragement about computing.
slides.plain: Feedback research shows that specific comments about the task and strategy help learning more than general praise.

qa.q: What if my child asks me for help and I don’t know the answer?
qa.a: Perfect: say “Let’s find out.” Ask them to explain the code line by line; they often spot the bug themselves.

slides.alt: Slide 24: YOUR ROLE How you can help, no coding needed Ask for a demo: “Show me what you made.” Ask about the bug, not the score: “What went wrong? How did you find it?” Praise strategies and effort, not “being a natural.” Protect 15 minutes a week for homework, at a regular time. Encourage everyone equally: girls hear less encouragement than boys. Come to the showcase at the end of…

slides.title: Safe, private and inclusive by design
slides.source: Federal Trade Commission (2025); AAP Council on Communications and Media (2016); Okabe & Ito (2008).
slides.say: Privacy: the course uses only offline apps, so no child creates an account, enters an email or uploads anything. Programs ask for nicknames or favorite colors, never real names or addresses. This is deliberate: the federal COPPA rule (updated in 2025) requires online services to get verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children under 13, and we prefer not to collect anything at all. Screen time: the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends consistent family limits for school-age children that protect sleep, physical activity and family time; our sessions include a stretch break, the 20-20-20 eye rule and unplugged activities. Inclusion: all materials use the Okabe–Ito color-blind-safe palette with icons and words alongside color, a highly legible font designed by the Braille Institute, and a dyslexia-friendly edition on request.
slides.plain: The 2016 pediatric guidance does not set a single number of hours for this age; it asks families to make a plan. One hour of creative coding a week plus 15 minutes of homework is a small part of a week.

qa.q: Will my child’s photo or work be posted online?
qa.a: No. Showcases happen on screen at home, and nothing is uploaded.

slides.title: Common questions
slides.say: These are the four questions parents ask most often. Keep answers short and invite follow-ups. If a question comes up that the evidence cannot answer, say so: “Research doesn’t tell us that yet.”

qa.q: What if my child loses interest?
qa.a: It happens. Children choose their projects, which helps, and each level is a natural stopping point.

qa.q: Is this better than an online course?
qa.a: Different: a small group, a familiar adult, no accounts, and a lot of talking and pair work, which research supports.

slides.alt: Slide 26: QUESTIONS Common questions Isn’t 10 too young? More screen time? No. Scratch was designed for this age. One hour a week, with breaks and games. Won’t AI make this pointless? I can’t code. Can I help? Someone has to understand and check Yes: ask questions and praise effort. AI’s work.

slides.title: Next steps
slides.say: Close by thanking parents again. Summarize in one sentence: coding is worth learning for its own sake; the research gives us good reasons to teach it through projects, pairs and debugging; and we are honest about what it will and will not do. Then open the floor.

qa.q: Can siblings join?
qa.a: The group is up to four children so everyone gets attention; ask, and we will see what is possible.

  • Ask about the bug, not the score: “What went wrong? How did you find it?”

  • Praise strategies and effort, not “being a natural.”

  • Protect 15 minutes a week for homework, at a regular time.

safety_html:
• No accounts, no logins, no email addresses.

  • Nicknames only; programs never ask for personal information.

  • Nothing is uploaded; projects stay on the computers in the room.

  • Screen breaks every session, plus unplugged activities.

  • Color-blind-safe materials and a dyslexia-friendly edition.
